posts.author: dave battin
posts.content_md: when i have completed coating a plate, i place it under the incandescing yellow light(clear so you can see the filament), if i look at the light after it passes through the plate you can easily tell if the coating is acceptable or flawed (by viewing the shadow cast onto white paper)...........

posts.author: Tom B.
posts.content_md: I guess this shows up thickness variations well? I wonder why this works. Maybe with more insight into what's going on, the inspection technique can be improved. I expect it's related to those patterns seen on the bottom of swimming pools (caustics) where small waves create ripply bright and dark patterns. Anybody that knows anything about optics care to comment?

posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md:
I know there isn't supposed to be a discussion regarding these tips, but this does leave some questions un-answered.

I can see that it would show variations in emulsion thickness which is what caustics are (in a sense). They're variations in density that cause light to be bent in different directions by different parts of the emulsion.

[here's a link to a caustic generator](http://www.lysator.liu.se/~kand/caustics/) if you want to play with some.

This technique would also more easily reveal dust in the emulsion since it's often easier to see the shadow of something rather than trying to focus on a mostly clear plate when looking through the plate at your safelight.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md: Perhaps an Integraf laser diode would be useful. It is about 660nm and with the lens removed any dust would show up as Newton Rings. At 660nm you should not have any fogging.

posts.author: dave battin
posts.content_md: the ability to see the dust is only a side benefit, the contour of the coating is what you are looking to see, even ripples across the plate, if there is a deviation you will see it!

posts.author: Martin
posts.content_md:
> **dave battin:** the ability to see the dust is only a side benefit, the contour of the coating is what you are looking to see, even ripples across the plate, if there is a deviation you will see it!

Confirmed.

We're doing this with a sodium vapor lamp. 589nm provides excellent visibility of those phenomenons. At the same time most recording materials (photopolymers, silver halide, DCG) have little sensitivity at that wavelength.
